strengths: Addresses a practical and comparatively underexplored problem: feedforward, cross-scene 3D Gaussian reconstruction from images containing transient distractors.
The training-time mask refinement, reference selection, and Gaussian pruning form a coherent end-to-end framework covering both training and inference.

Reported improvements are substantial: on the five-scene benchmark, the training method improves MVSplat from 15.45 to 21.02 PSNR, and the full method reaches 21.74. Component ablations generally support the proposed design.
Includes comparisons with several distractor-handling approaches, fine-tuning experiments, qualitative examples, and some analysis of reference-count and threshold choices.
weaknesses: The central claim that the generalizable masks outperform scene-specific methods is not quantitatively evaluated. Figure 6 provides only selected qualitative examples, with no mask ground truth, IoU/F1, comprehensive test set, or failure analysis.

The evaluation is too limited for the breadth of the claims. The principal quantitative results cover only five RobustNeRF scenes, the two held-out outdoor scenes appear mainly in fine-tuning results, and the synthetic datasets receive only qualitative comparisons. No uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or statistical analysis are reported.

The reference-selection protocol explicitly constructs query-centered pools containing both distractor-heavy and some distractor-free images. This favorable curation does not establish performance with naturally occurring or randomly sampled pools, while comparisons do not fully control for the larger candidate-image budget and additional inference computation.

Important technical definitions are ambiguous or apparently inconsistent. In particular, Eq. 7 takes a union of warped all-one masks, which represents coverage by at least one reference, whereas the text says it identifies regions absent from all references. Mask conventions and the exact segmentation-based filling and pruning rules are insufficiently formalized.

Reproducibility is poor. The supplied manuscript repeatedly refers to an appendix that is absent, while training schedules, dataset construction details, most thresholds, entity-filling criteria, implementation choices, and evaluation sample counts are missing. Code and models are only promised for future release.

Efficiency comparisons are incomplete because Entity Segmentation is precomputed and cached, and its preprocessing cost is not fully included. The two-stage method also evaluates additional candidate views, so the reported rendering-time comparison does not capture total end-to-end cost.

The method relies substantially on pretrained entity segmentation and hand-designed mask operations, yet lacks ablations across segmentation models or evidence that it handles distractors that segmentation does not cleanly partition. Common occlusion is acknowledged as a failure case without a systematic robustness evaluation.

Overall, the task is useful and the reported gains are promising, but unsupported headline claims, protocol concerns, technical ambiguity, and missing reproducibility information prevent the evidence from meeting a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies a practical and relatively underexplored problem: feed-forward, cross-scene 3D Gaussian reconstruction from images containing transient distractors.
The proposed system addresses both training-time robustness and inference-time artifacts through reference-based mask refinement, reference scoring, and Gaussian pruning.
Reported improvements over retrained MVSplat and adapted masking baselines are sizable; the component ablations indicate that both the training and inference modules contribute.
The qualitative examples generally support the claim that the method reduces ghosting and preserves more static-scene content than residual-only masking.
weaknesses: The central mask-accuracy claim is unsupported quantitatively. The paper claims to outperform scene-specific methods, but provides only a small qualitative comparison in Figure 6, with no mask ground truth, IoU/F1 measurements, or systematic evaluation.

The empirical scope is too limited for the broad generalization claims. Real-data training uses a small collection of On-the-go scenes, while aggregate testing covers only five scenes; results lack multiple runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests.

The inference protocol is favorable to the proposed method: the candidate pool is selected relative to each query and is explicitly constructed to contain some distractor-free images. The authors acknowledge that deployment may use an arbitrary pool, but never evaluate that realistic setting.

The baseline comparisons are difficult to interpret. Scene-specific methods are transplanted into MVSplat as masking components rather than evaluated in their native formulations, and essential implementation details needed to assess whether these adaptations are faithful are absent. Comparisons with models pretrained on different datasets also confound method and training data.
The synthetic evaluation is only qualitative despite being described as extensive. Dataset construction, distractor placement, split sizes, and quantitative results are all missing.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript repeatedly refers to an Appendix that is not present in the 13-page PDF, leaving dataset sizes, training schedules, thresholds, segmentation/refinement rules, pruning criteria, hardware, and baseline adaptations unspecified. Code and models are only promised for future release.

Several technical definitions are ambiguous or potentially inconsistent. In Equation 7, the union of warped all-one masks appears to represent regions visible in at least one reference, whereas the text describes regions absent from all references. Equation 10 does not clearly define scoring across the heterogeneous masks assigned to selected and unselected images.

The efficiency analysis is incomplete: it reports a single latency number without hardware, resolution, memory, preprocessing cost, or a clear accounting of all coarse reconstructions and segmentation operations required by two-stage inference.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. Numerous grammatical errors, inconsistent notation, underspecified equations, and very small qualitative panels impede verification of the method and results. strengths: Addresses a practical and relatively underexplored problem: feed-forward, cross-scene 3D Gaussian reconstruction from images containing transient distractors.

The proposed framework is coherent, combining reference-based training masks, mask refinement, reference selection, and 3D Gaussian pruning to address both training-time instability and inference-time artifacts.

Reported improvements are substantial: DGGS-TR raises mean PSNR from 15.45 for retrained MVSplat and 19.29 for the strongest adapted distractor baseline to 21.02, while the full inference framework reaches 21.74.

Component ablations provide useful evidence: reference-based mask prediction produces the largest gain, with additional improvements from refinement, auxiliary supervision, reference scoring, and pruning.
The experiments include unseen indoor and outdoor scenes, comparisons with several relevant baselines, fine-tuning experiments, qualitative examples, and an efficiency measurement.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too limited for the strength of the claims. The main quantitative result averages only five test scenes, reports no per-scene results, variance, multiple seeds, or statistical uncertainty, and evaluates synthetic data only qualitatively.

The evaluation reference pools are constructed around each query and deliberately guaranteed to include some relatively distractor-free images. This favors the reference-selection mechanism and does not establish robustness when every available reference is heavily corrupted or when a query-independent stream supplies the pool, as envisioned for practical use.

The central claim that the method predicts masks more accurately than scene-specific approaches is supported only by a small qualitative figure. No ground-truth mask benchmark, IoU, precision/recall, or boundary metric is reported.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript. Numerous essential details—dataset construction, training schedules, baseline adaptations, thresholds, pruning and occlusion rules, and additional results—are deferred to an appendix, but the PDF contains no appendix. Code and models are only promised.

Several technical operations are underspecified or potentially inconsistent. In particular, Eq. 7 uses a union of warped all-one masks while the text says it identifies regions absent from all references, apparently requiring a complement; the subsequent decoupling/recombination and Gaussian-pruning procedures are not formally defined.

The comparison to scene-specific methods is difficult to interpret because those methods are transplanted into a substantially different cross-scene training regime and may not constitute faithful or well-tuned implementations. Stronger controls using identical segmentation priors and oracle or ground-truth masks would clarify where the gains originate.

The two-stage inference gains are modest relative to the training contribution, while requiring twice running the reconstruction model and external entity segmentation. The timing table lacks hardware, resolution, preprocessing, memory, and end-to-end latency details.

Overall, the work is promising and technically plausible, but the missing quantitative mask validation, favorable reference-pool protocol, narrow evaluation, and absent implementation details leave the central generalization claims insufficiently established for acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and relatively underexplored problem: generalizable 3D Gaussian reconstruction when transient distractors occur during both training and inference.

The proposed framework is coherent and modular, combining reference-guided mask correction, mask refinement, reference scoring, and Gaussian pruning; it can plausibly be integrated into existing generalizable 3DGS systems.

Results on the real-data benchmark are promising: under the reported common training setup, DGGS-TR improves mean PSNR from 15.45 for MVSplat and 19.29 for the strongest adapted masking baseline to 21.02, while the full inference framework reaches 21.74.

The paper provides useful component ablations, segmentation-model variants, reference-count analysis, efficiency measurements, synthetic experiments, fine-tuning results, and explicit failure cases. Qualitative examples generally support improved artifact suppression.
weaknesses: A central claim—that the feed-forward masks outperform scene-specific distractor-removal methods—is not quantitatively evaluated. The paper reports no mask IoU, precision, recall, or boundary metric despite having synthetic ground-truth masks and apparently paired clean/clutter data; the claim rests on a few qualitative examples.

The experimental scope is narrow for a generalizable reconstruction claim: training uses roughly ten scenes from one real dataset, evaluation covers only two held-out outdoor scenes and a small indoor benchmark, all at 192×256 resolution, and no variation across random seeds or uncertainty estimates is reported.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. Pretrained MVSplat was trained on large clean Re10K data whereas DGGS is trained on domain-relevant distractor data, and adapted scene-specific baselines are materially modified—for example, NeRF-HuGS omits Nerfacto—so these results do not necessarily represent the original methods' capabilities.

The inference comparison gives DGGS access to K=8 candidate images while ordinary baselines use N=4. Comparing against N=8 directly does not isolate the scoring strategy; random subset selection, pose-coverage selection, image-quality heuristics, segmentation-based selection, and an oracle selector under the same candidate budget are missing. Moreover, evaluation pools are deliberately constructed to contain both distractor-rich and relatively clean images near each target view, which may overstate robustness in unconstrained capture.

The method description has important ambiguities. In particular, Eq. 6 unions warped all-one masks but describes the result as regions absent from all references, which appears inconsistent without a missing complement or a clearer mask convention. The rules for entity filling, common-occlusion detection, and Gaussian-to-mask pruning are also insufficiently specified for confident reproduction.

The synthetic benchmark pastes COCO objects independently into 2D views and is evaluated against only pretrained MVSplat, making the large reported gain difficult to interpret. Strong adapted baselines, realistic occlusion/compositing, and quantitative tests stratified by distractor size and frequency are absent.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is only promised after publication, key robust-mask thresholds are deferred to prior work, and the paper omits sufficient optimizer, scheduling, sampling, loss-weighting, segmentation-threshold, dataset-size, and end-to-end latency details. Segmentation is precomputed, so the headline timing does not reflect the complete pipeline.

The approach fundamentally depends on at least one reference revealing occluded content and fails under common occlusion, limiting the strength of claims about distractor-free reconstruction in general in-the-wild settings. This limitation is acknowledged but not systematically quantified.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant and underexplored problem: handling transient distractors in feed-forward, cross-scene 3D Gaussian reconstruction during both training and inference.
The proposed framework is modular and conceptually sensible, combining reference-guided mask refinement, candidate-reference scoring, and Gaussian pruning with an existing MVSplat backbone.

Experiments include real and synthetic data, component ablations, fine-tuning studies, efficiency measurements, and qualitative failure cases. The reported gains over retrained MVSplat variants are substantial for the training-time method.
weaknesses: A central claim—that the feed-forward masks outperform scene-specific distractor-removal methods—is not quantitatively evaluated. No mask IoU, precision, recall, or boundary metric is reported, even though the synthetic construction provides ground-truth masks; the claim rests on a few qualitative examples.

The comparisons to scene-specific methods are not fully convincing. Several methods are transplanted into MVSplat outside their intended optimization setting, and the NeRF-HuGS adaptation explicitly removes Nerfacto, an important part of that method. Their resulting underperformance does not establish superiority over the original approaches.

The inference comparison is confounded by additional test-time observations: DGGS examines a pool of K=8 images to select N=4, whereas primary baselines receive only N images. Showing that directly feeding eight images to DGGS-TR is worse does not replace comparisons against random subset selection, alternative quality selectors, repeated subsets, or an oracle selector under the same eight-image budget.

The evaluation is narrow and difficult to interpret. Training uses only a small collection of On-the-go scenes for 10K iterations, per-scene results are incompletely reported, uncertainty across runs is absent, and the paper does not evaluate whether its masking harms performance on standard clean generalizable-reconstruction benchmarks.

The synthetic benchmark is insufficiently realistic: COCO objects are pasted independently into 2D frames with random positions and rotations rather than rendered from a coherent dynamic 3D process. Surprisingly, its available ground-truth masks are not used to validate mask prediction.

Important methodological details are ambiguous or missing. The final refined mask is not precisely defined; Eq. 6 and its explanation appear inconsistent about visible versus absent regions; Eq. 9 does not clearly specify per-image scoring; distractor pruning and common-occlusion detection are described only informally; and several loss weights, thresholds, sampling details, and optimizer settings are unspecified.

The broad claims of generalizable distractor removal and pseudo-completion exceed the evidence. Quantitative inference gains on the main benchmark are relatively modest, quantitative DGGS results are omitted on two On-the-go test scenes because evaluation views contain distractors, and the method demonstrably fails when distractors occlude regions in all references.
Reproducibility is currently limited because code is only promised after publication, while the description and appendix do not provide enough detail to reconstruct several core operations reliably.

strengths: The paper identifies a practical and relatively underexplored problem: feed-forward, generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting in the presence of transient distractors during both training and inference.

DGGS presents a coherent framework combining reference-consistency-based mask prediction, mask refinement, reference scoring/reselection, and Gaussian pruning. The components are well motivated by the failure modes of generalizable 3DGS.

The main results are strong: on the reported five-scene RobustNeRF evaluation, DGGS improves mean PSNR from 15.45 for retrained MVSplat to 21.74, while also improving SSIM and LPIPS. It also outperforms MVSplat augmented with several established distractor-handling methods.

The component ablations are informative. Reference-based mask prediction provides the largest gain, while mask refinement, auxiliary supervision, reference scoring, and pruning each offer additional improvements. The study also examines segmentation backbones, mask fusion, reference counts, efficiency, and synthetic-to-real transfer.

Qualitative examples generally support the quantitative findings, showing cleaner reconstructions, fewer distractor artifacts, and improved detail. The paper also reports meaningful failure cases involving regions occluded in all references.
The approach remains feed-forward and incurs only a moderate reported runtime increase over MVSplat, making the contribution relevant to practical sparse-view reconstruction.
weaknesses: The real-world evaluation is limited. Training uses roughly ten sequences from one dataset, and the central quantitative test is based on only a handful of scenes. Broader evaluation across additional independently collected datasets, capture devices, distractor types, and outdoor scenes is needed to establish generalization convincingly.

The claim that the feed-forward masks outperform scene-specific distractor-removal methods is supported mainly by qualitative examples. No mask IoU, precision/recall, or boundary metric is reported, even though the synthetic construction should make quantitative mask evaluation possible.

Some comparisons are difficult to interpret. Pretrained generalizable models use different training data, while the distractor-free competitors are adaptations of scene-specific methods inside MVSplat rather than their native systems. These are useful comparisons, but they do not by themselves establish broad superiority over prior work.

The evaluation pool is constructed from views closest to each target and is deliberately made to contain both distractor-heavy and relatively clean images. This favors the proposed reference-reselection mechanism and does not demonstrate performance when all candidate views contain substantial or correlated occlusion. The paper acknowledges this failure mode but does not quantify robustness as occlusion coverage increases.

The synthetic distractors are created through 2D object compositing and may not reproduce realistic cross-view geometry, illumination, occlusion, or motion. Results on this benchmark may therefore overestimate performance in unconstrained captures.

Results omit uncertainty estimates, multiple training seeds, and statistical significance. Per-scene results are also incomplete for the main five-scene aggregate, making it difficult to determine whether improvements are consistent or driven by selected scenes.

Reproducibility is only moderate: the code is promised upon publication, several implementation choices and thresholds are not fully specified, and parts of the mathematical description and notation are ambiguous. The writing also contains frequent grammatical issues and overstrong claims.

The contribution is technically useful but primarily combines several heuristic modules around an existing MVSplat backbone. Thus, while the overall system contribution is meaningful, the algorithmic novelty of the individual components is moderate.
